title: Build hierarchy with weight and color, not size
principle: Refactoring UI’s public tip lineage (Wathan/Schoger): relying on font size alone for hierarchy is a common failure. Use color and weight—typically two or three text colors (primary dark, secondary grey, ancillary lighter)—and keep size steps few. On colored backgrounds, never use raw grey text; reduce opacity of white or pick a hue-matched mute instead.
procedure: Audit text roles: primary / secondary / ancillary—assign color+weight before touching font sizes.
Limit yourself to two or three type sizes; push contrast through weight and ink value.
On colored surfaces, replace grey with white-at-opacity or a hand-picked tint of the background hue.
Map actions to a hierarchy pyramid: one primary, few secondary, tertiary as links.
Screenshot-critic: can you still parse hierarchy if all sizes were equalized?
examplePrompts:
Refactor typography hierarchy (Refactoring UI public tips):
- Roles: primary / secondary / ancillary via color+weight, not five font sizes.
- Max three sizes on this view.
- If text sits on a colored background, forbid grey—use white opacity or hue-matched mute.
- Buttons: one solid primary, outline/low-contrast secondary, link-style tertiary.
Return token changes + rationale.
This card uses size for every level and grey labels on a blue header. Fix hierarchy with weight/color; hue-match the muted header text.
promptWhy: Caps size steps so models stop shouting with 5xl/4xl/3xl ladders.
Names the grey-on-color failure mode explicitly—models love soft grey everywhere.
tips: Public Medium tip ‘7 practical tips for cheating at design’ and refactoringui.com free previews cover these rules.
De-emphasize to emphasize: quiet surroundings make the primary loud without neon.
Labels are a last resort—prefer content that explains itself.
No endorsement of the paid book; only public tips paraphrased.

provenance.statement: Design Catalog editorial synthesis of the cited public sources; contracts and decision paths are our implementation guidance, not quotations or author endorsements.

useWhen: Can someone find the next action without reading every label?
avoidWhen: Do not add a new visual hierarchy to a screen whose real problem is missing information.
inputs: A concrete user problem and the current artifact
Constraints, existing behavior and source attribution to preserve
agentContract.output: A bounded application of “Build hierarchy with weight and color, not size” with before/after evidence and remaining limitations.
acceptance: At 390px and 1280px, identify the primary action without scrolling past decorative material; preserve text contrast and the same reading order.

stateRequirements.responsive: Check 390px and desktop plus 200% zoom; preserve reading order, wrap long text and keep actions reachable.
stateRequirements.accessibility: Use semantic headings and native controls, visible labels and focus; normal text contrast at least 4.5:1.
stateRequirements.keyboard: Complete the primary action using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space; no pointer-only information or focus trap.
stateRequirements.reducedMotion: Remove nonessential movement; preserve all state and information without waiting for animation.
stateRequirements.loading: Show pending feedback only during real work; retain context and allow navigation away.
stateRequirements.empty: Distinguish no content from no matching results; explain how to proceed or reset filters.
stateRequirements.error: Explain the failed action, retain user input and offer recovery; never claim success on failure.
stateRequirements.interruption: A newer action wins; cancel or ignore stale results and keep controls responsive.
stateRequirements.stateChange: Announce important results politely without moving focus unexpectedly.

compatibility.rule: Start with one technique. Add at most one companion for a distinct unsolved problem; candidates are suggestions, not verified compatibility.
conflicts: Two techniques changing the same visual role require an explicit winner.
Do not combine multiple entrance or attention effects on one target.
Aesthetic subtraction must not remove semantics, feedback or attribution.
compatibility.stop: One action leads; supporting information is still readable.

comparison.bad: Six equally prominent buttons make the reader compare every option before acting.
comparison.good: One clear next step, quieter alternatives, and nearby context make the choice legible.
comparison.impact: One action leads; supporting information is still readable.
